newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: LME copper seen groping for direction - trade.
newsitem.headline: LME copper seen groping for direction - trade.

text.p: The London Metal Exchange (LME) base metal complex will probably drift sideways later on Tuesday with the market groping for direction due to the grip of the seasonal summer doldrums, traders said on Tuesday.
"It needs some sort of direction," a senior trader for a metal dealing firm in Singapore said. "It'll probably do nothing in the morning and wait for the U.S. to come in."
"It's just drifting along because of the summer holidays," a Japanese trader added.
The summer swoon holding sway over the market has prompted several players to unload material and mark time on the sidelines, one trader said.
"You can play marbles at the moment. It's so quiet and will probably remain so in London this afternoon," he said.
"The (copper) market may try the lower end of its recent range with initial support pegged at $2,355/65 (a tonne)," LME brokers Brandeis said in its daily review.
Rudolf Wolff said in its own report that "we expect further consolidation" in the red metal and "await the confirmed move out of the initial $2,390-$2,420 range."

Asian base metal business remained quiet, with three-month copper being quoted by regional dealers slightly firmer at around US$2,380/85 a tonne at 0230 GMT against the late indication in London on Monday of $2,380.
The Far East trade was keeping an eye more on the steadily rising amounts of zinc in the LME's Singapore warehouse.
The volume of zinc has already reached 31,350 tonnes on Monday, up sharply from the 11,900 tonnes in the middle of May.
Traders estimate about 15,000-20,000 tonnes remain off-warrant in Singapore warehouses and that around 5,000 to 8,000 tonnes of zinc is said to be on its way here from China.
"Demand in the region is pretty good. Zinc is supposed to be in deficit here," one trader said.
The large volume of zinc in the city-state kept premiums low, with those for 25-kg ingots being quoted at $3-$5 a tonne against $25-$30 at the end of May.

The movement by China of zinc to Singapore was touched off by the sharp rise in zinc prices which is said to be poised to touch the key $1,500 a tonne level soon because of a severe shortage of the metal in the second half of 1997.
Three-month zinc was quoted by the trade at 0230 GMT at about $1,449/54 a tonne, up from the late quote in London on Monday of $1,446/50 a tonne.
"Zinc is at a pretty critical level," one dealer said, adding though that any fall in the price would immediately find "good consumer buying."
